To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
foreign subsidiaries pay more, work harder and earn less, but they do not reduce market efficiency in Poland.
foreign subsidiaries pay higher wages and use more capital per employee, earn lower ROAs and contribute with higher employment and labor productivity growth than domestic firms.

foreign subsidiaries in the Polish manufacturing sector pay more (in terms of wages and capital), they earn less (in the sense of lower ROAs), but work harder (in the sense that they have higher TFPs) and contribute to the economy through higher employment growth than their domestic counterparts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the entry and presence of multinational enterprises (MNEs) on domestic firms and industries.
the impact of the foreign direct investment (FDI) on the host country.
the effects of foreign direct investment on the Polish economy, the performance of foreign subsidiaries and the market efficiency effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
foreign subsidiaries are more productive than other firms in Poland and do not seem to have a negative impact on market efficiency.
the foreign presence in the Polish manufacturing has been beneficial for Poland.
the evidence on foreign subsidiaries performance and market efficiency is mixed, but the net effect is positive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
foreign subsidiaries in emerging markets do not necessarily contribute to the host country in a way that is expected by economic theory.
the foreign subsidiaries are more efficient than domestic firms, but the market efficiency effects are limited to intra-industry spilling over.

foreign subsidiaries in the Polish manufacturing are not only more productive but they also seem to be more competitive and more likely to contribute to market efficiency than their domestic counterparts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
foreign owned firms in emerging markets do not seem to be more efficient than domestic firms.
foreign firms have not only been more productive than domestic firms in Poland but also more efficient in terms of resource allocation.
foreign subsidiaries in emerging markets are a heterogeneous group and that the effects they have on the host economy are highly industry- and mode-specific.
